extracted.intended_audience: general readers of humorous travel literature / readers of 19th‑century satire
extracted.subtask_description: A comic travel narrative that records observations, anecdotes, and satire about foreign places and customs, using irony, exaggeration, and mock‑erudition to undercut romantic or reverent accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell a tale worth the listening to
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories and anecdotes should be worth hearing — they must entertain and engage the reader rather than merely exist as filler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain opens by wishing the old parties could 'tell a tale worth the listening to.' Example use: prioritize incidents with ironic or revealing payoff. Anti-pattern: long, aimless historical lists with no comic or thematic payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground humor in concrete historical detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specific dates, places, and historical facts to lend authenticity and to set up comic contrasts with modern sensibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain chronicles Notre Dame's successive buildings (A.D. 300, 500, 1100) to create a sense of weight that he then undercuts humorously. Guidance: specific detail increases credibility and makes irony sharper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ironic understatement and deadpan delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: State surprising facts or judgments in a mildly phrased, 'measured' way to generate comic effect by contrast with the subject's gravity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The ground ought to be measurably sacred by this time, one would think.' Use calm register to describe absurdity; anti-pattern: overwrought declarations that remove the ironic gap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirize institutions by juxtaposing sanctity and moral corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Expose hypocrisy by placing religious or civic pomp beside acts that contradict their supposed values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain points out that a murderer 'could wipe the stain from his name' by building a church addition. Use such juxtapositions to reveal moral absurdities; avoid blunt denunciation — let contrast do the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward relics and miraculous claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat displays of relics or miracle stories with skeptical amusement, calling attention to their curious or theatrical aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain lists nails, a fragment of the cross, and an angel‑diving story; labels the taste 'somewhat singular.' Guidance: catalog the relics and the improbabilities to elicit comic disbelief rather than sermonizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vivid, concrete, and sometimes grotesque description
rubrics_metrics.description: Deploy sensory, unflinching detail (sights, textures, odors) to produce a strong emotional — often comic or unsettling — effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Morgue description (drowned man swollen, purple, water trickling) uses detail to force reader reaction and then to reflect on spectatorship. Guidance: specifics make the scene palpable and heighten ironic commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose voyeurism and social habits through comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare public morbid curiosity to ordinary entertainments to criticize or gently mock audiences' motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain compares regular Morgue‑visitors to people who go to the theatre every night. Use analogies to everyday habits to reveal uncomfortable truths about spectatorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self‑deprecating narrator voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Have the narrator admit follies or small failures in a comic way to build rapport and produce humor from human weakness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain: 'I committed an error which any donkey might make...' — this kind of line diffuses pretension and invites laughter. Use sparing, candid admissions rather than constant self‑mockery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration and spectacle for comic climax
rubrics_metrics.description: Amplify an action or scene (through hyperbole and piling on of details) to produce a spectacularly comic image or finale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blondin's thousand Roman candles, 'a blinding blaze of glory,' and the can‑can's grand final rush are built by escalating details. Use crescendo to reach comic peak; avoid overuse that blunts impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise, blunt comic definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer short, plainspoken definitions of local customs or phenomena that highlight their oddness and provoke amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain defines the can‑can: 'The idea of it is to dance as wildly... expose yourself...' A pithy definition both informs and satirizes. Use sparing, memorable formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mocking reverence for high art and patrons
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique artistic worship by pointing out how gratitude to patrons can slide into 'nauseous adulation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain finds old masters' flattery of patrons more prominent than their art. Use mild moralizing plus wit to undermine lofty claims of greatness and expose social pressures behind art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ironically framed national comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare national traits or customs in a way that praises and punctures both sides, often ending with a wry concession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain contrasts American bluntness with French superiority in certain things: 'We are measurably superior... but they are immeasurably our betters in others.' Use balanced irony rather than obvious jingoism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect and expose commercial frauds with a practical test
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify petty deceptions (signs, advertising) and suggest simple, practical ways to test the claims, exposing the imposture to comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'English Spoken Here' sign and the fake 'American drinks' menu — Twain's party tests by ordering typical drinks. Guidance: show the scam and provide a quick 'trial' that proves it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deflate romantic myths with direct observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Counter sentimental or travel‑book romanticizations by reporting the plain, often unromantic reality observed firsthand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain's grisettes are 'homely' rather than the romantic ideal. Use measured description and contrast with received stories to puncture myths; avoid mean‑spiritedness — the tone is corrective and comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody sentimental retellings to undermine mawkishness
rubrics_metrics.description: Retell famous romantic tales in a brusque, ironic voice to show how sentimentality can obscure inconvenient facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain's 'Story of Abelard and Heloise' strips away 'nauseous sentimentality' and casts Abelard as a 'dastardly seducer.' Use selective fact emphasis and comic moral commentary to rescue realism from sentimentality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mock‑academic or bureaucratic structure for comic contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitate the formal structures of scholarship or officialdom (heads, subheads, cold rhetoric) to make passionate material seem absurdly dry or vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain contrasts Heloise's passionate letters with Abelard's 'finished essays, divided... into heads and sub‑heads.' Use mismatched register to reveal character and produce comic distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight 'general effect' in large‑scale aesthetics
rubrics_metrics.description: When describing grand designs (parks, palaces), emphasize the overall effect and scale rather than minute realism, and use that to shape reader awe or gentle critique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On Versailles Twain notes 'They seek the general effect' when defending formal shrubbery. Use this as a principle for describing large, designed spaces: prioritize sweeping impressions, then add ironic human details.
